title: All (of), whole, every, each
subtitle: all the time / the whole city / every six months
summary: Place all correctly in a sentence and choose between all, whole, entire, every and each.

lesson.heading: all after the noun or pronoun
lesson.text: We can put all after the noun or pronoun it refers to instead of in front of it. The meaning is the same.

examples.text: His songs **all** sound much the same to me.
We **all** think Kushi's working too hard.

lesson.heading: Where all goes in the verb phrase
lesson.text: When all follows the subject, it comes after the verb be, and after the first auxiliary verb if there is one - never in front of it.

examples.text: They **are all** going to Athens during the vacation.
You **should all** have three question papers.
We have **all been** involved in the decision.

lesson.note: In spoken English 'You all should have ...' is possible for particular emphasis.

lesson.heading: not all (of) or none of?

left.label: not all (of) - some, but not every one
left.text: For negatives we normally use not all (of) rather than all ... not.
examples: **Not all (of)** my cousins were at the wedding.

right.label: none of - not a single one
examples: **None of** my cousins were at the wedding.

lesson.note: all ... not does occur in informal spoken English, but not all (of) is the safe choice.

lesson.heading: all and whole with singular nouns
lesson.text: Before singular countable nouns we normally use the whole rather than all the. Entire works in the same position, immediately before the noun.

examples.text: They weren't able to stay for **the whole** concert.
examples.note: rather than ... for all the concert

examples.text: **The whole** / **entire** building has recently been renovated.
After the fire **the whole** city was covered in dust.

lesson.note: But we do say all + day / week / night / month / winter, all the time, all the way. All October and all 21st May are not used, and all Monday / Tuesday only in informal contexts.

lesson.heading: all (of) or whole with plural nouns?

left.label: all (of) the + plural = every one in the group
examples: **All (of) the** towns had their electricity cut off.
The new rail network links **all of the** towns in the region.

right.label: whole + plural = some of them, completely affected
examples: After the storm, **whole** towns were left without electricity.
**Whole** areas of the country have been devastated by the floods, although others haven't had rain for months.

lesson.note: We don't say ~~whole the towns~~. In informal speech all the can also be used with things we see as made up of parts: all the house / city / department.

lesson.heading: When to prefer every
lesson.text: Every and each are often interchangeable, but every is the one we want with almost / virtually + noun (the group as a whole), with a plural noun after a number, and with abstract uncountable nouns to mean 'complete' or 'total'.

examples.text: I go to the dentist **every** six months.
She has **every** chance of success in her application for the job.
examples.note: also: every confidence / hope / reason / sympathy

lesson.note: Every is also fixed in phrases for regular events: every other (kilometre), every single (day), every so often, every few (months), every now and again.

lesson.heading: When to prefer each
lesson.text: We use each before a noun or before one when we are talking about both people or things in a pair, and each can also stand alone as a pronoun.

examples.text: I only had two suitcases, but **each one** weighed over 20 kilos.
In a rugby league game **each** side has 13 players.
I asked many people and **each** gave the same answer.

lesson.text: When either word fits, each makes the listener picture the members separately, while every is closer to 'all of them together'.

exercises.prompt: You ___ stay for dinner if you want.
exercises.explanation: all comes after the modal or first auxiliary verb, not before it.

exercises.prompt: We ___ going to be late if we don't hurry.

exercises.statement: They all are going to Athens during the vacation.
exercises.explanation: They are all going to Athens during the vacation. all goes after the first auxiliary verb.

exercises.prompt: We have ___ involved in the decision.
exercises.explanation: all goes after the first auxiliary (have) and before the rest of the verb phrase.
Before a singular countable noun we use the whole rather than all the.

exercises.prompt: ___ of the country have been devastated by the floods, although others haven't had rain for months.
exercises.explanation: whole + plural noun means some areas were completely affected - all areas would mean every area in the country.

exercises.prompt: When I picked up the book I found that ___ had been ripped out. There wasn't a single one left.
exercises.explanation: Not one page was left, so we mean every page: all of the pages.

exercises.prompt: Which word fits the gap better - every or each?

items.text: I had ___ reason to believe that she would keep my secret.
We've discussed the problem in virtually ___ meeting for the last year.
They had to take out ___ single part of the engine and clean it.
You should take two tablets ___ four hours.
In a rugby league game ___ side has 13 players.
The two girls walked in, ___ one carrying a bouquet of flowers.
The ten lucky winners will ___ receive £1,000.

exercises.prompt: She has ___ chance of success in her application for the job.
exercises.explanation: With abstract nouns like chance, hope, reason and sympathy we use every to mean 'complete' or 'total'.

exercises.prompt: I only had two suitcases, but ___ weighed over 20 kilos.
exercises.explanation: For both things in a pair we use each (one), not every.

exercises.prompt: Fortunately, ___ the food usually gets eaten, so I have plenty left for the rest of the week.
exercises.explanation: Negatives are made with not all (of) rather than all ... not.

exercises.prompt: Put the last sentence of the blog post in order.
exercises.answer: The rest of us all had a great time and we spent the whole evening talking.
exercises.explanation: all follows the subject and comes before the main verb had; before a singular noun we use the whole.
